messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajesh had always been a pillar of strength for his community, dedicating his life to helping others through his work at a local non-profit organization. But that all changed one fateful night when he was brutally raped by someone he trusted. The trauma of that event has left an indelible mark on Rajesh's life, and now, two years later, he finds himself struggling to cope with the aftermath. As he sits in his small apartment, surrounded by the familiar sounds of the city outside, Rajesh can't shake off the feeling of being permanently damaged. He believes that his reactions since the event show that he is a lousy coper, unable to deal with even the smallest challenges without becoming overwhelmed. This negative self-perception has led him to engage in maladaptive strategies, such as hurting himself physically to release overwhelming feelings. "I feel like I'm drowning," he says, "and this is the only way I can keep my head above water." But these attempts at coping have only served to reinforce his negative appraisals of himself. Rajesh has come to believe that he will never be able to feel normal emotions again, that he is lost in a sea of numbness. This sense of emotional paralysis has made him even more vigilant, always on the lookout for potential threats. He listens intently for sounds that might mean someone is entering his home, and startles with alarm when someone touches him unexpectedly. Even everyday noises can send him into a panic, as he becomes convinced that danger lurks around every corner. The memories of that traumatic night continue to haunt Rajesh, often triggered by auditory cues that transport him back to the scene of the crime. He hears the sound of footsteps outside his apartment and is instantly flooded with images of that terrible night. When these memories resurface, he feels a searing physical pain in the same parts of his body as during the event, a cruel reminder of what was done to him. Unable to verbalize his emotions or process the trauma, Rajesh becomes even more withdrawn, unable to shake off the feeling of being an outsider. As the days turn into weeks, and the weeks into months, Rajesh's maladaptive strategies have taken on a life of their own. He has become accustomed to sitting with his back against a wall, constantly scanning the room for potential threats. His non-profit work has begun to suffer as well, as he finds it increasingly difficult to connect with others or form meaningful relationships. "I feel like I'm living in a constant state of hypervigilance," he says, "like I'm waiting for the other shoe to drop." Despite his best efforts, Rajesh can't seem to break free from this cycle of negativity and fear. His negative appraisals have become a self-fulfilling prophecy, reinforcing his maladaptive strategies and perpetuating the memories that haunt him. As he looks around his cluttered apartment, Rajesh knows that he needs help to break this cycle, but he's terrified of what might happen if he opens up about his past. It was only when he found himself unable to attend a community event, overcome with anxiety at the thought of being in a crowded space, that Rajesh realized he needed professional help. He is now seeking therapy, hoping to learn how to manage his symptoms and find a way out of this darkness. But for now, he remains trapped in this cycle of fear and self-doubt, unsure of what the future holds or whether he will ever be able to heal.
